draft.title: The world after the First World War
card: The First World War ended in 1918. About nine to ten million soldiers had died, and many civilians as well. Families and towns across Europe were left grieving.
Four empires collapsed: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires. Their old rulers lost power, and new states appeared in their place.
Many European countries borrowed heavily to pay for the war. They came out of it in debt, and their farms, factories and cities were damaged.
Grief, debt and the collapse of old rulers left Europe unstable. These conditions set up the tensions of the next two decades.
draft.remember: The war left Europe grieving, in debt and without its old empires, so it was unstable.

a.q: Which of these was a direct result of the First World War for Europe?
opts: Several empires collapsed and new states appeared
Every country became richer from selling weapons
The old empires gained more land and power
Europe's debts were cleared by the end of the war
a.why: The German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires all fell, and new states replaced them. Europe came out of the war in debt, not richer, so the other options are wrong.
a.clue: Think about what happened to the old rulers.

b.q: Why did the state of Europe after 1918 make future tensions more likely?
opts: Debt, loss of life and new states left Europe unstable
The war had left every country equally strong and secure
Europe had no armies left, so nobody could trade
The war settled all disputes over borders for good
b.why: Heavy debt, millions of deaths and the fall of old rulers left Europe unsettled. The idea that the war settled everything is tempting, but new states and new borders created fresh disputes.
b.clue: Look at what the war left behind, not at who won.

a.best: Several empires collapsed and new states appeared

b.best: Debt, loss of life and new states left Europe unstable

proposal.title: The world after the First World War
card: The First World War ended in 1918. About nine to ten million soldiers had died, and many civilians as well. Families and towns across Europe were left grieving.
Four empires collapsed: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires. New states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia appeared in their place, with new and untested governments.
Winners and losers alike came out of the war in debt. Britain and France had borrowed heavily, much of it from the United States, and parts of France and Belgium were badly damaged.
Grief, debt and new, unsettled states left Europe unstable. These conditions set up the tensions of the next two decades.
proposal.remember: The war left Europe grieving, in debt and without its old empires, so it was unstable.

a.q: Which statement best describes Europe's finances after the war?
opts: Winners and losers alike were left in debt
Only the defeated powers were left in debt
The United States owed Britain and France large sums
Britain and France paid for the war from their savings
a.why: Both sides came out of the war in debt. Britain and France were on the winning side, yet they had borrowed heavily, much of it from the United States. So it was not only the losers who owed money, and the lending ran from the United States to Europe, not the other way.
a.clue: Did winning the war mean a country had no debts?

b.q: A historian says Europe in 1919 was 'a house built on sand'. Which point best supports this view?
opts: Weak new states and heavy debts left Europe unstable
Russia's empire grew to fill the space left behind
The winning powers came out of the war rich and secure
The old empires survived and blocked any change
b.why: Sand is an unsteady base, so the historian means Europe was unstable. New, untested states and heavy debts support that. The idea that the winners were rich and secure is tempting, but Britain and France were deeply in debt too.
b.clue: Sand shifts. Look for what made Europe unsteady.

a.best: Winners and losers alike were left in debt

b.best: Weak new states and heavy debts left Europe unstable
